summary: - _(c) Pass any such further orders as this Commission may deem just and appropriate in the facts and circumstances of the case.”_ (m) The Commission relied upon in certain cases, whose details are given in paragraph 21 of the Review Petition, were at varied and incomplete stages of progress, with pleadings pending or substantive hearing yet to commence in most of them. Yet they have been invoked to justify the issuance of a show cause notice under Section 19 of the Act. These matters pertain to commercial and banking disputes commonly encountered in electricity trading, several of which involve counterclaims by KEIPL (e.g., 94/MP/2023), and that, if allowed, would yield a net financial credit in its favour. However, instead of awaiting the outcome of these cases, the Commission is said to have acted on presumptive liability and prejudged sub-judice disputes, including in cases where KEIPL’s replies were not on record (Petition Nos. 288/MP/2024 and 261/MP/2024), contrary to natural justice and amounting to an error apparent on the face of the record. 5. The matter was heard on 18.9.2025. After the hearing, the order in the matter was reserved. 8. We have examined the submissions made by the parties and have perused the record, including the impugned order. _**(** 1) The Commission shall exercise jurisdiction to review its own orders, decisions, and directions in accordance with Clause (f) of sub-section (1) of Section 94 of the Act read with Section 114 and Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code._ _(2) Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision, or order of the Commission, from which no appeal has been preferred, may file a review petition on the following grounds within forty days of the making of such decision, direction, or order:_ Business) Regulations, 2023 (for short, ‘2023 COB Regulations’), seeking review of the impugned order dated 19.5.2025 in Petition No. 306/MP/2022. Under Section 94(1)(f) of the Act, the Commission is vested with the same powers as are vested in a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, in the matter of “reviewing its decision, directions and orders”. Regulation 52(2) of the 2023 COB Regulations provides that an aggrieved person can seek the review of a direction, decision or order of the Commission on grounds analogous to those set out under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. _41. After hearing the learned senior counsel for the parties, the Commission directed to list the matter for further hearing/compliance on 26.12.2024, and in the meantime, the Respondent may comply with the direction dated 1.5.2024._ _**The Commission, however, made it amply clear that such compliance by the Respondent, if any, will be without prejudice to its liability arising out of the non-compliance with the direction dated 1.5.2024 in the stipulated timeframe. The Respondent was also permitted to file its brief note of submissions** ._ _43. The matter was last heard on 26.12.2024._ _**During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that as of date, the principal amount of Rs. 20.75 crores and Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) of Rs.34 crores are required to be paid by Respondent No.1 (KEIPL)** ._ _**Learned counsel submitted that vide Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 1.5.2024, Respondent No.1 was directed to make the payment of the entire principal outstanding in two equated monthly instalments** ._ _**However, no compliance has been made to the said direction of the Commission by Respondent No.1, KEIPL.** Learned senior counsel for the Respondent No. 1 submitted that KEIPL remains committed to resolving the disputes amicably and in a manner that ensures finality. However, the Petitioner’s conduct, including the pursuit of parallel proceedings and imposition of unwarranted charges, has rendered the situation_ _untenable and has made it impossible to redress the issues. Learned senior counsel added that necessary directions be passed for amicable settlement of the matter(s), whereby parties can sit together and arrive at a full and final settlement, which results in payment to the Petitioners, while also ensuring the withdrawal of all the cases and action on the blacklisting by the Petitioner._ _52. We now proceed to examine whether the Petitioner has made out the case under Section 19 of the Act against the Respondent. Section 19(1)(a) of the Act provides that “where the licencee, in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission, makes willful and prolonged default in doing anything required of him by or under_ 18. In these circumstances, the Review Petitioner`s plea that the Commission has relied upon, undecided cases while issuing the show cause notice, is 22. With regard to the contention of KEIPL seeking reference of the disputes in Petition No. 306/MP/2022 to arbitration in terms of the arbitration clause in the Agreement(s) with UPCL and in light of Section 79(1)(f) of the Act and no reasoned finding being returned, we are of the view that the said aspect was duly considered by the Commission in the impugned order wherein the Commission clearly observed that the present matter involves the revocation of the trading licence and the Petition was not filed under Section 79(1) (f) of the Act and as such it was not appropriate to refer the dispute/issue to arbitration. Moreover, the revocation of the licence entails the exercise of regulatory powers, which is non-arbitrable. The Review Petitioner in this Review Petition is reiterating its submissions already considered in the impugned order, which is impermissible in review.
title: Review Petition under Section 94(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, read with Regulation 52 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023, seeking review of the order dated 19.05.2025 passed in Petition No. 306/MP/2022.
